title: T.R.O.Y. and Tom Scott
hook: That horn on T.R.O.Y. isn't a rap record.
voiceover: That horn on T.R.O.Y. isn't a rap record. Pete Rock built the whole thing off Tom Scott's 'Today,' a 1967 jazz cut most heads have never heard. He looped four bars of that saxophone, sped it up a touch, and let it breathe. Here's what nobody says: the song is a eulogy. Trouble T Roy of Heavy D's crew died in 1990, and Pete made the beat to grieve. That's why it aches. The sadness was in the sax before the words. Save this, then go pull up Tom Scott and hear where the tears came from.
caption: Pete Rock made T.R.O.Y. to mourn a friend — Trouble T Roy from Heavy D & the Boyz, gone in 1990. The ache you feel is Tom Scott's 1967 saxophone on 'Today,' looped and lifted. Grief you can dance to. 🎷 What's the saddest beat that still fills a floor for you? Drop it below and I'll pull the sample next week.

title: Synthetic Substitution
hook: One drum break. Hundreds of records. It starts here.
voiceover: One drum break. Hundreds of records. It starts here. In 1973 a singer named Melvin Bliss cut a soul 45 called 'Reward.' Nobody bought it. But flip it over and the B-side, 'Synthetic Substitution,' opens with a drum pattern so clean that producers have been borrowing it for 40 years. Ultramagnetic MCs cut it on 'Ego Trippin'.' From there it spread everywhere. I still drop that pattern in a jersey club edit at 2am and the room moves the same way it did in the Bronx. One failed single, one immortal break. Name a record you've heard it on.
caption: Melvin Bliss put out one soul 45 in 1973 called 'Reward.' Flopped. But the B-side, 'Synthetic Substitution,' hides one of the most-sampled drum breaks ever pressed. Ultramagnetic MCs cut it, then hundreds followed. I still fold it into jersey club edits at 2am. 🥁 Name a record you've caught this break in — I'll pin the deepest cut.

title: Reading the room in three records
hook: Your first three records decide the whole night.
voiceover: Your first three records decide the whole night. Most DJs walk in and play what they planned. I don't touch my plan until I've read the room. Record one, I watch feet, not phones. Record two, I test the energy a notch up and see who follows. Record three, I commit to the lane the crowd already showed me. If they moved on the soulful one, I'm not forcing drill for another hour. Reading beats picking. The set you prepped at home is a guess. The room is the answer. What's your opening record when you don't know the crowd?
caption: The set you built at home is a hypothesis. The room is the data. I don't commit to a lane until three records tell me who's actually in front of me — feet first, phones never. Prep hard, then be willing to throw the plan out. 🎧 DJs: what's your safe opening record when you walk in cold?

title: Juicy and Mtume
hook: Juicy isn't Biggie's melody. It's a 1983 record.
voiceover: Juicy isn't Biggie's melody. It's a 1983 record. That warm groove is Mtume's 'Juicy Fruit,' a slow-jam that was already a hit before Big said a word. Puff and Poke from Trackmasters replayed it, tightened the tempo, and turned a bedroom song into a block anthem. Here's the flip that matters: they kept the sweetness but changed the story. Mtume was singing about a woman. Biggie sang it to everybody who ever doubted him. Same chords, brand-new meaning. That's a real flip. Save this, then pull up 'Juicy Fruit' and hear the original spell before the words.
caption: Before 'Juicy' was Biggie's origin story it was Mtume's 1983 slow jam 'Juicy Fruit.' Trackmasters replayed the groove, tightened it, and flipped a love song into a message to everyone who ever counted him out. Same chords, brand-new meaning — that's the art of the flip. 🍑 What's your favorite sample that completely changed what a song meant?

title: The Meters Rejuvenation
hook: If you own one funk record, own this.
voiceover: If you own one funk record, own this. The Meters, 'Rejuvenation,' 1974, out of New Orleans. Zigaboo Modeliste is the drummer every sampler has borrowed from, and this is where his pocket lives. Look for the original Reprise pressing — that's the one that sounds right, and copies still turn up in the soul bins. As a DJ this record earns its spot because the drums are already loop-ready; you barely have to touch them. 'Just Kissed My Baby' alone is worth the crate space. Send this to the one friend who still buys vinyl.
caption: New Orleans funk, 1974. Zigaboo Modeliste's drum pocket on The Meters' 'Rejuvenation' is a sampler's dream — loop-ready straight off the wax. Look for the original Reprise pressing and don't sleep on 'Just Kissed My Baby.' A record that earns its crate space every single set. 💿 Tag the one friend who still buys vinyl.

title: Playing unfamiliar gear
hook: You've got five minutes on gear you've never touched.
voiceover: You've got five minutes on gear you've never touched. Every working DJ walks into this — a booth with a mixer you don't know and a line already forming. Here's my checklist. One, find the gain and the master before anything, so you never redline the room. Two, check the crossfader curve and the cue button — that's how you hear before they do. Three, play one record you know cold so your ears calibrate to the system, not the song. Never learn the gear on a banger. Learn it on something safe, then swing. What's the worst booth you've ever been handed?
caption: Every touring DJ has walked into a booth with a mixer they've never seen and a line already forming. Gain and master first, curve and cue second, calibrate on a record you know cold — never on a banger. Small habits, saved nights. 🎛️ What's the worst booth setup you've ever been handed?

title: Resurrection at 32
hook: Thirty-two years ago, one man made this whole album.
voiceover: Thirty-two years ago, one man made this whole album. Common dropped 'Resurrection' on October 25th, 1994, and every beat on it came from one producer: No I.D., out of Chicago. Everyone posts 'I Used to Love H.E.R.' Here's the part nobody posts. That same No I.D. took a teenager under his wing a few years later and taught him how to chop soul records. That kid was Kanye West. So the Chicago sound that took over rap traces straight back to this album's producer. One mentor, two eras. Where were you the first time you heard 'I Used to Love H.E.R.'?
caption: October 25, 1994: Common's 'Resurrection,' produced start to finish by Chicago's No I.D. Everyone quotes 'I Used to Love H.E.R.' Fewer know No I.D. later mentored a teenage Kanye West and taught him to chop soul. The whole Chicago takeover starts on this record. 🎶 Where were you the first time you heard 'I Used to Love H.E.R.'?

title: Can I Kick It and Lou Reed
hook: 'Can I Kick It?' is really Lou Reed.
voiceover: 'Can I Kick It?' is really Lou Reed. That bounce under the song is the bassline from his 'Walk on the Wild Side,' 1972. Q-Tip looped it, dropped a Lonnie Smith horn on top, and made it feel brand new. But because they used Reed's track so plainly, he reportedly collected 100 percent of the publishing. Tribe made a classic and earned nothing off that beat. The lesson still holds: clear your samples or somebody else eats. Save this, then play the two back to back and hear how little Tip had to change.
caption: Q-Tip built 'Can I Kick It?' on the bassline from Lou Reed's 1972 'Walk on the Wild Side' — used it so plainly that Reed reportedly took 100% of the publishing. Tribe made a classic and earned nothing off the beat. Clear your samples, always. 🎸 Play both back to back — barely anything changed.

title: Skull Snaps break
hook: A mystery band made rap's favorite drum break.
voiceover: A mystery band made rap's favorite drum break. In 1973 a group called Skull Snaps put out one self-titled album and vanished. Nobody could tell you who they were for years. But the first seconds of 'It's a New Day' — that dry, snapping drum intro — became one of the most-sampled breaks in the music. Gang Starr rode it on 'Take It Personal.' So did half the boom-bap era. I still fold it under amapiano when I want that dusty knock against a clean log drum. One album, one break, generations deep. Name a record you know is built on Skull Snaps.
caption: Skull Snaps dropped one self-titled album in 1973 and disappeared — for years nobody even knew who they were. The dry drum intro to 'It's a New Day' became one of rap's most-sampled breaks. Gang Starr's 'Take It Personal' and half the boom-bap era ran it. 🥁 Name a record you know is built on Skull Snaps.

title: The bass-swap EQ transition
hook: Two basslines fighting is why your mix sounds muddy.
voiceover: Two basslines fighting is why your mix sounds muddy. When you blend two records with the low end up on both, the kicks and bass collide and the whole thing turns to mush. The fix is simple and it's the move that separates DJs from playlists. As you bring the new record in, pull the bass all the way down on it. Let only the top and mids ride over the outgoing track. Then, right on the phrase change, kill the bass on the old one and open it on the new. Clean handoff, no mud. One bassline at a time — always. Try it this weekend.
caption: Muddy mixes almost always come from two basslines fighting. Pull the low end off the incoming record, ride the tops over the outgoing track, then swap the bass on the phrase change. One bassline at a time. It's the difference between DJing and pressing play. 🎚️ Try it this weekend and report back.

title: Gold Digger and Ray Charles
hook: That Gold Digger hook is a 1954 gospel record.
voiceover: That Gold Digger hook is a 1954 gospel record. Kanye built it on Ray Charles' 'I Got a Woman,' where Ray took a church song and made it secular — scandalous at the time. But here's the flip inside the flip. Instead of just looping Ray, Kanye had Jamie Foxx re-sing the opening lines. Foxx had just played Ray in the movie, so the voice you hear isn't Ray at all — it's an actor doing him. A sample of a sample of a performance. Save this, then play Ray's 1954 version and hear where the whole thing was born.
caption: Kanye built 'Gold Digger' on Ray Charles' 1954 'I Got a Woman' — then had Jamie Foxx (fresh off playing Ray in the movie) re-sing the opening lines. The voice you know isn't even Ray. A sample of a performance of a legend. 🎹 What's your favorite Kanye soul flip?

title: Dorothy Ashby Afro-Harping
hook: Rap's most sampled harp. Most heads missed it.
voiceover: Rap's most sampled harp. Most heads missed it. Dorothy Ashby, 'Afro-Harping,' 1968, on Cadet out of Chicago. A jazz harpist — not an instrument you expect in a break — but those cascading strings have been chopped by Pete Rock, Madlib, Flying Lotus, more. Look for the Cadet pressing with the blue label; reissues float around but the original mono has the weight. As a DJ I keep it for texture — a harp roll over a drum loop does something no synth can. A woman with a harp quietly shaped decades of beats. What's the record you'd never sell?
caption: Dorothy Ashby played jazz harp — not an instrument you expect in a break — but 'Afro-Harping' (Cadet, 1968) has been chopped by Pete Rock, Madlib and Flying Lotus. Look for the original Cadet pressing; the mono has the weight. A quiet record that shaped loud music. 🎼 What's the record you'd never sell?

title: Trainwreck recovery
hook: Your mix just fell apart. Don't stop the record.
voiceover: Your mix just fell apart. Don't stop the record. Every DJ trainwrecks — two beats sliding out of sync, the room about to notice. The amateur move is to yank the fader and kill it, which tells everyone something broke. The pro move is to commit. Cut the bad record fast on a hard drum hit, so it lands like a choice, not a mistake. Or throw a quick echo out and pull the tempo back into place by ear. The crowd forgives anything you play through with confidence. Panic is the only real mistake. How do you save a mix live?
caption: Every DJ trainwrecks. The tell isn't the mistake — it's the panic. Cut the bad record on a hard drum hit so it lands like a choice, or throw an echo and pull it back by ear. Play through with confidence and the crowd never knows. 🎧 How do you save a mix live?

title: The Diary at 32
hook: Thirty-two years ago, Houston made a masterpiece.
voiceover: Thirty-two years ago, Houston made a masterpiece. Scarface dropped 'The Diary' on October 18th, 1994 — 'I Seen a Man Die,' some of the heaviest writing the South ever put on wax. Everyone posts the lyrics. Here's the part nobody posts. A young engineer named Mike Dean shaped the sound of this record. That same Mike Dean went on to become the sonic hand behind Kanye, Travis Scott, and half of modern rap. The synths you hear on today's biggest albums trace back to Rap-A-Lot in Houston. One studio, a whole lineage. Where does 'The Diary' rank for you?
caption: October 18, 1994: Scarface's 'The Diary' — 'I Seen a Man Die' still hits like few records ever have. The detail people skip: a young engineer named Mike Dean shaped this album, then went on to become the sonic hand behind Kanye and Travis Scott. Houston lineage runs deep. 🎶 Where does 'The Diary' rank for you?

title: California Love and Joe Cocker
hook: California Love is built on a white rock singer.
voiceover: California Love is built on a white rock singer. That synth-funk monster under 2Pac is Joe Cocker's 'Woman to Woman,' a 1972 record most Pac fans have never heard. Dr. Dre looped the groove, and Roger Troutman laid that talkbox on top — the robot voice everybody sings. Here's what Dre changed: he took a loose, bluesy jam and made it march. Tightened the drums, squared the bassline, turned a 70s rock cut into a West Coast anthem. Save this, then play Joe Cocker's 'Woman to Woman' and find the exact four bars Dre lifted.
caption: That synth-funk monster under 2Pac's 'California Love' is Joe Cocker's 1972 'Woman to Woman.' Dr. Dre tightened the drums, squared the bass, and Roger Troutman laid the talkbox on top. A 70s rock jam turned into a West Coast anthem. 🌴 Play the Cocker cut and find the exact four bars Dre lifted.

title: The Champ by The Mohawks
hook: One organ groove from London runs through rap.
voiceover: One organ groove from London runs through rap. In 1968 a British studio band called The Mohawks cut an instrumental called 'The Champ' — swirling organ over a tough drum break. It became one of the most-sampled records on earth. Producers from New York to London have cut it up for decades, from early hip-hop to UK rave to grime. When I bridge a boom-bap set into something faster, that organ stab is my passport — it fits every tempo. A break made in England that helped build American rap. Name the record where you first heard 'The Champ.'
caption: In 1968 a British studio band called The Mohawks cut 'The Champ' — swirling organ over a tough break — and it became one of the most-sampled records on earth. From New York rap to UK rave to grime, that organ stab travels every tempo. 🎹 Name the record where you first heard 'The Champ.'

title: Phrasing on the eight
hook: Count to eight before you touch that fader.
voiceover: Count to eight before you touch that fader. The reason some mixes feel surgical and some feel sloppy is phrasing. Dance records are built in 8-bar and 16-bar blocks. If you bring the new track in mid-phrase, the two songs argue. If you line up the tops of the phrases, they hold hands. So count. Find bar one of the drop, find bar one on the incoming record, and start your blend so both hit the change together. It's not talent, it's counting. Once your ear locks to the 8, you'll never mix blind again. Try counting your next transition out loud.
caption: The difference between surgical and sloppy is phrasing. Dance records move in 8s and 16s — line up the tops of the phrases and two songs hold hands instead of arguing. Count bar one on both, blend into the change. It's not talent, it's counting. 🎧 Try counting your next transition out loud.

title: Hotline Bling and Timmy Thomas
hook: Hotline Bling is a 1972 protest record underneath.
voiceover: Hotline Bling is a 1972 protest record underneath. That skeletal beat — the cheap organ, the drum-machine click — is Timmy Thomas's 'Why Can't We Live Together,' a plea for peace recorded on a home organ with a rhythm preset. Drake's producer Nineteen85 barely touched it. He looped it, added Drake, and left the loneliness in. Here's the flip: Thomas made an empty-sounding record to sound like the world after war. Drake used that same emptiness to sound like a man alone with his phone. Same hollow, new heartbreak. Save this, then play Timmy Thomas and hear 1972 in a 2015 hit.
caption: Drake's 'Hotline Bling' is Timmy Thomas's 1972 'Why Can't We Live Together' — a peace anthem recorded on a home organ with a drum preset. Nineteen85 barely touched it, kept the loneliness, and made it about a phone. Same hollow, new heartbreak. 📞 Play the 1972 original and hear 2015 already inside it.

title: Lonnie Liston Smith Expansions
hook: One record taught rap how to sound cosmic.
voiceover: One record taught rap how to sound cosmic. Lonnie Liston Smith, 'Expansions,' 1975, on Flying Dutchman. The title track is pure spiritual jazz-funk — Fender Rhodes, a bassline that never quits, and a groove producers keep coming back to. Stetsasonic flipped it for 'Talkin' All That Jazz,' and house DJs have never let it go. Look for the original Flying Dutchman pressing; RCA handled distribution, so both labels show up on legit copies. As a DJ this is a peak-of-the-night record — put it on and watch the floor float. Warm, deep, timeless. Send this to the friend who thinks jazz can't move a room.
caption: Lonnie Liston Smith's 'Expansions' (Flying Dutchman, 1975) taught rap and house how to float — Rhodes, an endless bassline, pure spiritual jazz-funk. Stetsasonic flipped it; DJs never let it go. Original pressings show both Flying Dutchman and RCA. A peak-of-the-night record. ✨ Tag the friend who says jazz can't move a room.

title: Handling requests
hook: A request can wreck your set. Here's the move.
voiceover: A request can wreck your set. Here's the move. Someone leans into the booth and names a song. You can't just slam it on — wrong key, wrong tempo, wrong moment, and you lose the room you built. But you don't want to be the DJ who ignores people either. So I do two things. One, I say 'I got you' and mean it — then I find the version or the tempo that fits my lane. Two, if it doesn't fit at all, I play something adjacent that scratches the same itch. Serve the feeling, not the exact file. How do you handle requests?
caption: A request can wreck the room you built — wrong key, wrong tempo, wrong moment. But ignoring people isn't the move either. Say 'I got you,' then find the version that fits your lane, or play something adjacent that scratches the same itch. Serve the feeling, not the file. 🎧 How do you handle requests?

title: good kid maad city at 14
hook: Fourteen years ago, this wasn't just an album.
voiceover: Fourteen years ago, this wasn't just an album. Kendrick Lamar dropped 'good kid, m.A.A.d city' on October 22nd, 2012. Everyone posts the tracklist. Here's what people skip: the full title is 'A Short Film by Kendrick Lamar.' It's not a playlist of singles — it's one story, start to finish. And those voicemails between songs, the mom and dad you hear? Those are his actual parents, Kenny and Paula, threading the whole thing into a movie for your ears. Listen in order or you're watching a film out of sequence. Where were you when this dropped?
caption: October 22, 2012: Kendrick's 'good kid, m.A.A.d city.' Shuffle it and you're watching a film out of order. 🎬 Where were you when this dropped?

title: Mind Playing Tricks and Isaac Hayes
hook: Rap's scariest record rides a sweet soul song.
voiceover: Rap's scariest record rides a sweet soul song. Geto Boys' 'Mind Playing Tricks on Me,' 1991 — paranoia, insomnia, the mind coming apart. Under all that dread is Isaac Hayes, 'Hung Up on My Baby,' a gentle 1974 soundtrack cut. That warm, looping guitar was written for a love scene. Willie D and the crew flipped its meaning completely — the softness makes the fear worse. That's the trick of a great sample: the mood underneath fights the words on top, and the tension is the whole song. Save this, then play Isaac Hayes and feel how calm the source really is.
caption: Geto Boys' 'Mind Playing Tricks on Me' (1991) — rap's great paranoia record — rides Isaac Hayes' gentle 1974 'Hung Up on My Baby,' a guitar line written for a love scene. The softness makes the dread worse. Mood underneath fighting words on top — that's the whole song. 🎸 Play the Hayes original and feel how calm it is.

title: Hihache in Paris
hook: American musicians in Paris made this drum break.
voiceover: American musicians in Paris made this drum break. The Lafayette Afro Rock Band were from New York, but they moved to France, and in 1973 they cut 'Hihache' — a raw, rolling drum break that traveled back across the ocean and into rap. Wreckx-n-Effect rode it on 'Rump Shaker.' Public Enemy, Biz Markie, LL — all pulled from this band. I still edit that break into club sets because it swings harder than a drum machine ever will. A break that crossed an ocean twice to get to your speakers. Name a record you've caught it in.
caption: The Lafayette Afro Rock Band were New Yorkers who moved to Paris and cut 'Hihache' in 1973 — a rolling break that traveled back into rap. Wreckx-n-Effect's 'Rump Shaker,' Public Enemy, Biz Markie, LL all pulled from it. Still swings harder than any drum machine. 🥁 Name a record you've caught it in.

title: Rap acapella over log drum
hook: A 90s rap vocal over an amapiano log drum.
voiceover: A 90s rap vocal over an amapiano log drum. This is the move that gets both rooms — the heads who want bars and the crowd who wants that South African bounce. Grab a clean acapella, something everybody knows. Find an amapiano groove in a compatible key and tempo — usually you're pitching the rap up or the piano down a touch to meet. Then drop the vocal in the log drum's breathing room, not on top of the busy parts. Let the drum lead, let the voice float. Two eras, one floor. What acapella would you try first?
caption: The transition that keeps both rooms: a clean 90s acapella over an amapiano log drum. Match key and tempo — usually pitch the rap up or the piano down — then drop the vocal in the drum's breathing room, not the busy parts. Two eras, one floor. 🎤 What acapella would you try first?

title: Accordion and Daedelus
hook: That accordion loop is a real instrument, once.
voiceover: That accordion loop is a real instrument, once. Madvillain's 'Accordion' — DOOM and Madlib, 2004 — sounds like a dusty old squeezebox. It's actually a 2002 record by Daedelus called 'Experience,' and that's a real accordion, played straight. Madlib slowed it, looped a few bars, and let DOOM ramble over it with no hook, no chorus, no rules. Here's the flip: Daedelus made a pretty, delicate piece. Madlib made it sound haunted just by slowing it down and adding dust. Speed is a mood. Save this, then play Daedelus and hear how bright the original really is.
caption: Madvillain's 'Accordion' (2004) samples Daedelus's 2002 'Experience' — a real accordion, played straight and bright. Madlib slowed it, added dust, and DOOM rambled over it with no hook, no rules. Speed is a mood: one slow-down turned pretty into haunted. 🎹 Play the Daedelus original and hear how light it started.

title: David Axelrod Song of Innocence
hook: Producers guard this record like a secret.
voiceover: Producers guard this record like a secret. David Axelrod, 'Song of Innocence,' 1968, on Capitol. Axelrod made cinematic funk — huge drums, dramatic strings, arrangements that sound like a film score for a movie that doesn't exist. DJ Shadow and a generation of diggers built careers out of records like this. Look for the original Capitol pressing with the rainbow rim label; the drums hit harder on the early cut. This isn't a party record — it's a producer's record, the kind you buy to sample or to study. Deep, heavy, essential. What's the record in your crate you'd never let a friend borrow?
caption: David Axelrod's 'Song of Innocence' (Capitol, 1968) is cinematic funk — huge drums, dramatic strings, a score for a film that doesn't exist. DJ Shadow and a generation of diggers built careers on records like this. Find the original Capitol rainbow-rim pressing; the drums hit harder. 💿 What's the record you'd never let a friend borrow?

title: The energy reset record
hook: Cool the room to keep the room.
voiceover: Cool the room to keep the room. New DJs think the job is to go up, up, up until the roof comes off. But a floor that never breathes gets tired, and tired means they leave. So I build in a reset — one record that pulls the energy down on purpose. Something warm and familiar, mid-tempo, that lets people talk, grab a drink, catch their breath. Then when I climb again, they climb with me. The dip is what makes the peak feel like a peak. Control the valley, own the mountain. What's your go-to reset record?
caption: New DJs chase the peak and never let the floor breathe — and a floor that never rests, leaves. Build a reset: one warm, mid-tempo record that lets people talk and catch their breath. The dip is what makes the next peak feel like a peak. 🎧 What's your go-to reset record?

title: Ironman at 30
hook: Thirty years ago, a 'solo' album that wasn't.
voiceover: Thirty years ago, a 'solo' album that wasn't. Ghostface Killah dropped 'Ironman' on October 29th, 1996. Everyone calls it his solo debut. Here's the part nobody posts: Raekwon and Cappadonna are on it so heavily it plays like a three-man group record. And the whole thing floats on old Delfonics soul — RZA drowned it in 70s Philly strings, and that became Ghost's signature sound forever after. A solo album built by a crew, powered by records your grandparents owned. That's Wu. Where does 'Ironman' sit in the Wu catalog for you?
caption: October 29, 1996: Ghostface Killah's 'Ironman.' Called a solo debut, but Raekwon and Cappadonna are on it so heavily it plays like a trio record — all floating on old Delfonics soul RZA drowned in 70s Philly strings. A solo album built by a crew. 🎶 Where does 'Ironman' sit in the Wu catalog for you?

title: Mass Appeal and Vic Juris
hook: Premier's cleanest loop is a jazz guitar record.
voiceover: Premier's cleanest loop is a jazz guitar record. Gang Starr's 'Mass Appeal,' 1994 — that bright, rolling melody everybody knows — comes from Vic Juris, a jazz guitarist, on a 1978 cut called 'Horizon Drive.' DJ Premier found a few bars, looped them, chopped in his scratches, and made one of the catchiest beats of the decade. Here's the Premier move: he never takes the obvious part. He digs for the two seconds nobody else would loop, then makes it feel inevitable. That's the craft. Save this, then play Vic Juris and try to spot the exact bars Preemo stole.
caption: Gang Starr's 'Mass Appeal' (1994) — that bright rolling loop — comes from jazz guitarist Vic Juris's 1978 'Horizon Drive.' Classic Premier: he never takes the obvious part, he digs for the two seconds no one else would loop and makes it feel inevitable. 🎸 Play the Juris cut and spot the bars Preemo lifted.

title: When the Levee Breaks
hook: The heaviest drums in rap came from a stairwell.
voiceover: The heaviest drums in rap came from a stairwell. In 1971 Led Zeppelin recorded 'When the Levee Breaks' with John Bonham's kit at the bottom of a stone staircase, mics hung high above. That's why those drums sound like a cannon in a cave. The Beastie Boys cut them on 'Rhymin and Stealin,' and producers have chased that sound ever since. When I want a break that fills a big room, this is it — nothing modern hits with that much air around it. A rock record, a staircase, and half of hip-hop's biggest drums. Name a track you've heard these drums in.
caption: Led Zeppelin recorded 'When the Levee Breaks' (1971) with Bonham's kit at the foot of a stone stairwell, mics hung high — that's why the drums sound like a cannon in a cave. Beastie Boys cut them on 'Rhymin & Stealin,' and producers have chased that air ever since. 🥁 Name a track you've heard these drums in.
